catalog_quote: Suprasegmental features are not mentioned in the Dictionary and Grammar and they are inadequately recorded in the field notes. However, it is clear that words have suprasegmental phonemes as a part of their makeup and that in many instances this is the sole phonemic contrast between words. These phonemes have been called "tone" because pitch seemed to be their most stable feature, but loudness (stress) is very much involved, and perhaps length as well. One noticeable feature is the way in which the toneme of a monosyllabic word affects the pitch and stress of the following word. The words listed below were studied both in isolation and in a frame--followed by the particle /ti/. In section 1 above two tonemes were listed, tentatively labelled high /´/ and low /`/. There are at least two tonemes, and one of them does seem to involve high pitch most of the time. But phonetically, there are a lot of up-glides [ˇ] and down-glides [ˆ] in the data and very few consistently low pitches other than on /ti/. The up-glides seem to be associated with slight lengthening of the vowel. Since the analysis of tone has barely been begun, the tone markings on the words given below are quasi-phonetic. They are only approximate because of free variation in the data, but the contrasts which they illustrate are real enough. There seem to be three tone patterns on monosyllabic words, three on disyllabic words, and many on trisyllabic words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kapau word prosody is analysed as lexical tone (tentatively two tonemes, high and low, contrasting minimal pairs such as /tʌ/ 'fire' vs 'this'); loudness/stress is described as bound up with the tonemes rather than as an independent, positionally fixed word stress; no rule for stress placement is given and the author says the analysis has barely begun. Elsewhere (p.96) /ɨ/ is said to be 'frequently stressed'. Lloyd 1973:40 independently states for Kapau 'Phonemic stress occurs, but has not been completely analysed.'
new_statements.exceptions: Toneme of a monosyllable perturbs pitch and stress of the following word (tested in frame with particle /ti/); up-glides associated with slight vowel lengthening; three tone patterns on monosyllables, three on disyllables, many on trisyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonemes; data studied in isolation and in a frame before /ti/. The Rosetta excerpt lacks pp. 103-109 (secs. 4.4 end, 5 Glottal stop, 6 Syllabic nasals), which by their titles do not treat stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe the language under the name Kapau (= Hamtai, hamt1247, ISO hmt); Healey's own data are from Slate Creek near Bulolo (1958) plus NTM materials from the Aseki/Morobe side; Lloyd 1973 calls the language relatively uniform dialectally. No sub-variety glottocode needed.

sources.note: sec. 2.31 Kapau phonology (pp. 39-40, following Healey 1958 ms): 'Phonemic stress occurs, but has not been completely analysed.' (p.40). Family summary p.87: 'Tone and stress are combined in a complex unit which usually occurs in connection with the grammatical stem.. Angaataha is like a "tone language" and the others are more "intonation languages".' p.95: Angan languages 'have complex supra-segmental systems, usually a combination of pitch and stress'.

sources.note: Silent on word stress; neither confirms nor contradicts Healey 1981 (tone/stress complex) or Lloyd 1973 ('phonemic stress occurs, but has not been completely analysed'). The orthography marks no stress or tone, which is consistent with Healey's remark that suprasegmentals were 'not mentioned in the Dictionary and Grammar'.
'14 consonants, 7 vowels, and two tones (rising and falling)', citing Healey 1981 p.95; nothing on stress.
